name: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate

lead: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is a fat-soluble form of vitamin C used in brightening and anti-ageing serums, positioned as a more stable alternative to L-ascorbic acid.
Studies are small and test whole regimens, so its own effect is not isolated.

paras: As an ascorbate ester it is used as an antioxidant and pigment-modulating vitamin C source; lab work shows it can degrade under oxidative stress unless stabilised.
Trials of products containing it report generally good tolerance; no specific serious safety signals were found in the sources reviewed.

lead: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate (THD ascorbate, THDA) is an oil-soluble ester derivative of vitamin C used in serums and moisturisers marketed for brightening and anti-ageing. It is used as an alternative to L-ascorbic acid, which is described as unstable and sometimes irritating at high concentrations [1][2].

Human data on THDA specifically are limited to small, mostly manufacturer-associated studies of multi-ingredient products. A 2021 laboratory study reported that it degrades rapidly under oxidative stress but can be stabilised by acetyl zingerone [3], and a 2024 randomized double-blind study compared THDA with and without acetyl zingerone on facial photoaging [4].

paras: THDA is an ascorbic acid ester designed to dissolve in oils, in contrast to water-soluble L-ascorbic acid. Vitamin C in general is described as labile, with oxidation accelerated by light, oxygen, heat and higher pH [5]. Studies of vitamin C in skin care frame delivery and instability as the main formulation challenges [2].

The studies below test products or regimens containing THDA and cannot attribute effects to it alone. A prospective open-label, evaluator-blinded study of a dual regimen including a 30% vitamin C formulation reported lightening of facial melasma over a summer [2]. Open-label trials of multi-ingredient regimens combining retinol and vitamin C, and of an anti-ageing moisturiser, reported improvements in hyperpigmentation and photodamage appearance [6][7]. A hydroquinone-free brightening product was assessed through melanogenesis inhibition in vitro and UV-induced hyperpigmentation in people [8]. A multicorrective product was assessed for dark circles and puffiness [9].

A 2021 study reported that THDA degrades rapidly under oxidative stress but could be stabilised by acetyl zingerone, with enhanced collagen production and antioxidant effects in vitro [3]. Acetyl zingerone is described as a photostable ingredient [10].

A 2024 prospective randomized double-blind comparative study examined topical acetyl zingerone with THDA versus THDA alone on facial photoaging [4]. An earlier double-blind half-face study tested a topical vitamin C preparation against vehicle for photodamage, though the abstract does not identify THDA as the test form [11]. Registered trials include an eye-serum study (n=35) for the periorbital area and an AI-personalised regimen study for photoaging in women (n=43) [12][13]. Many of these were run or supported by companies that make the products.
